rejected.title: Change and continuity in France
card: Change
Something that was different by 1795 from how it was in 1774. The privileges of the nobility and clergy were abolished, and the absolute monarchy ended.
Continuity
Something that stayed the same, or that the revolution failed to alter. Many people stayed poor, and women did not gain political rights.
Historians weigh both. A hope is an aim of the revolution, such as equality. An unmet hope points to continuity, but it can sit alongside real change.
A judgement about the revolution uses evidence of both change and continuity across the period 1774 to 1795.

a.q: Which of these is an example of change in France between 1774 and 1795?
opts: Noble and clergy privileges were abolished
Women still had no political rights
Many poor families still struggled for food
Equality was still out of reach for many
a.why: The abolition of privileges made France different from how it was in 1774, so it is change. The other three describe things that stayed the same or hopes that went unmet, which point to continuity.
a.clue: Which one describes something that ended, not something that stayed?

b.q: A student says the revolution brought only change to France by 1795. Which evidence from the period best challenges this claim?
opts: Women still lacked political rights in 1795
The absolute monarchy had ended by 1795
Nobles no longer held legal privileges
Louis XVI was no longer ruling France
b.why: Women still lacking political rights shows something that stayed the same, so it is continuity and challenges the claim. The end of the absolute monarchy and the other two options are real changes, so they support the claim instead.
b.clue: Look for the option that shows something that did not change.

a.best: Noble and clergy privileges were abolished

b.best: Women still lacked political rights in 1795

problems.detail: 'Most women did not gain political rights' suggests some women did. No French women gained formal political rights such as the vote in this period, and women's political clubs were banned in 1793. 'Women did not gain political rights' would be accurate.
'Hopes for equality were left unmet by many' is awkward. It reads as if many people left the hopes unmet, rather than that the hopes went unmet for many people.

'Where a hope was not met, the result was continuity, not change' is too absolute. An unmet hope can still sit alongside real change, so this oversimplifies how historians weigh change and continuity.

check.summary: Both intended answers are correct. The card wrongly implies some women gained political rights ('most women did not'), one distractor in question a is awkwardly worded, and the card's rule that an unmet hope always means continuity is oversimplified.

draft.title: Change and continuity in France
card: Change
Something that was different by 1795 from how it was in 1774. Feudal dues and noble privileges were abolished, and absolute monarchy ended.
Continuity
Something that stayed the same, or that the revolution failed to alter. Many people remained poor, and women did not gain political rights.
A hope is an aim of the revolution, such as equality. A change in law does not prove the hope was met, because people's lives may stay much the same.
A historian judges the revolution by weighing evidence of both change and continuity between 1774 and 1795. Real change can sit alongside unmet hopes.
draft.remember: Judge the revolution by weighing both: what changed in law and government, and what stayed the same in people's lives.

a.q: Which statement is the soundest judgement about France between 1774 and 1795?
opts: Law and government changed, but equality was not fully won
Law and government changed, so equality was fully achieved
Little changed, as the poor stayed poor under the new laws
Almost nothing changed, as privilege and monarchy survived
a.why: Privilege and absolute monarchy ended, which is change, but many hopes for equality were not met, which is continuity. The second option treats a change in law as proof that the hope was met. The third and fourth ignore the real change in law and government.
a.clue: A sound judgement weighs evidence of both, and a change in law does not prove a hope was met.

b.q: A student argues that equal rights in law meant equality in daily life by 1795. Which point best challenges this argument?
opts: Women did not gain political rights despite the new laws
Noble and clergy privileges were abolished in law
Feudal dues ended, so peasants owed nothing to lords
Absolute monarchy gave way to a republic in 1792
b.why: Women not gaining political rights shows that new laws did not give everyone equality, which is continuity. The other options are real changes in law and government, so they support the argument instead of challenging it.
b.clue: Which evidence shows a group left out of the new equality?
